title: “Workers unite the world”: how BMS answered a famous slogan
author: Editorial Desk
summary: In the 1950s the popular call was ‘Workers of the world, unite!’. BMS turned the sentence around.
body:
In the 1950s, the slogan most often raised at labour gatherings was *"Workers of the world, unite!"* BMS saw in it a call for disruption and class hatred. Its answer was to turn the sentence around: **"Workers unite the world."** The change is small in words and large in meaning, and it tells a good deal about how BMS understands the place of the worker in society.

## Where the slogan comes from

The older slogan is associated with the Marxist tradition of the labour movement, which sees society as divided into classes whose interests are in conflict. BMS's founding documents reject that view. *The Onward March of BMS* says the organisation was based on Bharatiya values and on integral humanism, rejected the class concept in favour of a "vertical arrangement of society", and opposed both capitalism and communism. BMS's website states its position more simply: it does not accept class struggle, and its fight is against injustice and exploitation, not against any class.

Its documents record that the 1955 slogan "Workers of the world, unite" was replaced with "Workers: unite the world". Biographical accounts credit Dattopant Thengadi with the reworking, and one describes it as a reworking of the Marxist call. Other replacements followed. One of them, translated from Hindi in the BMS history, runs roughly as: in the new era, he who earns will eat.

## Builders, not destroyers

The change is more than wordplay. In the first slogan, the worker's task is to unite across borders against a class enemy. In the second, the worker is a **builder**, whose labour has the power to bring a divided world together. Production, peace and cooperation come before conflict.

This is consistent with the BMS idea of a union as a partner in production. The organisation speaks of an "industrial family" and of workers taking part in industry with duties as well as rights. It also says that consumers and society are a "third party" that the union must keep in mind. A strike that stops production harms not only the employer but also the customer who needs the goods, the other workers whose jobs depend on the plant and the nation's economy. The slogan puts that thought in four words.

## A change you can hear

BMS's own account notes that it also replaced the cry of *Inquilab* at labour gatherings with *Vande Mataram* and *Bharat Mata ki Jai*. BMS says that "Bharat Mata Ki Jai" was a slogan unfamiliar in the labour field before it introduced it. A tribute written by a former BMS leader says the red flag gave way to a saffron flag and that Vishwakarma Jayanti was introduced as National Labour Day.

None of this is only about symbols. A movement's slogans shape who feels it is speaking for them. BMS's claim is that Indian labour found, through these changes, a voice that was its own and not borrowed from foreign movements. Critics from other labour traditions answer that national slogans can blur real conflicts of interest at the workplace. Readers can weigh both views, but it is useful to know what BMS intends by the change.

## The symbol that goes with the slogan

BMS's emblem makes the same point visually. According to the organisation, it combines an industrial wheel for industrialisation, a plough or agriculture motif and a human fist for the unity of workers. BMS's website draws attention to the opposable thumb in the fist, which its history describes as the origin of tools, and therefore of human construction. The flag is saffron. Together, the emblem and the slogan say that the worker is a creator of things.

## Not soft, but different

None of this means that BMS avoids struggle. It organises demonstrations, memoranda and, when needed, strikes. According to the BMS history, it took part in the 1963 Bombay Bundh as coordinator and in the 1974 railway strike as a constituent of the National Coordination Committee for Railwaymen's Struggle.

But it keeps a rule: demands must be firm, and methods must be constructive. *The Onward March of BMS* explains that BMS did not want a union that was merely agitational, and that as a nationalist organisation it should ensure that production is not hampered. BMS's website adds that strikes are a last resort after talks, negotiation and arbitration have failed, and that it opposes violence. The history also describes a posture towards governments that it calls "responsive cooperation": support where a measure helps workers, opposition where it harms them.

## A companion slogan

Another BMS line often heard at rallies is *Desh ke hit mein karenge kaam, kaam ka lenge poora daam*, which means: we will work in the interest of the country, and we will take full wages for the work. Placed beside "Workers unite the world", it shows the two halves of the BMS approach. The worker is a builder, and the builder has the right to be paid fully for what is built. A related line from the movement describes the spirit of its karyakartas as sacrifice, penance and martyrdom.

## The international angle

The slogan has had a second life at international forums. The BMS website mentions that it took part in BRICS events, including a 2024 labour convention in Russia, and that it leads the Indian workers' delegation at International Labour Organization conferences. At such forums BMS speaks of worker-centric cooperation among nations. That is the same thought in a global setting: if workers are builders, then the cooperation of workers across countries should be about building common prosperity, not about confrontation.

BMS's older international experience points the same way. One biography records that Thengadi led a BMS delegation to China in 1985, at the invitation of the Communist Party of China, which suggests that the slogan did not prevent engagement with unions of a different ideology.

## What remains to be asked

A slogan is a promise, and it is fair to ask how well a movement keeps it. For BMS, the test is whether its unions secure good wages and conditions for members while also keeping production and national interest in view, and whether it extends its work to the workers who are hardest to organise: contract workers, scheme workers, gig and platform workers and the self-employed artisans it calls the Vishwakarma sector. Later posts will look at these groups one by one.
